content: The scientific community is composed of all scientists and their relationships and interactions. It is typically divided into sub-communities, each focusing on a specific scientific field. For instance, within computer science, there exists a robotics community. Objectivity in science is expected to be achieved through the scientific method. Peer review, facilitated by discussions and debates in journals and conferences, plays a critical role in ensuring objectivity by maintaining the quality of research methodologies and the interpretation of results. Membership in the scientific community is generally determined by factors such as education, employment status, and institutional affiliation. Status within the community is strongly linked to an individual’s publication record. Sociological studies indicate that gender, race, and class may also influence one’s status in the community. Scientists are typically trained in academic settings, particularly through universities, and degrees in relevant scientific sub-disciplines are often prerequisites for membership in the corresponding scientific community. A PhD, with its emphasis on research, often serves as an entry point into the community. However, continued membership requires maintaining connections with other researchers through publications and conferences. After earning a PhD, academic scientists may pursue postdoctoral fellowships and eventually professorships. Others may find employment in industry, think tanks, or government roles. Independent researchers are often regarded with less prestige, although, in principle, scientists are judged based on the quality of their contributions. Members of the same scientific community do not necessarily work together, but communication is established through the dissemination of research findings and hypotheses in peer-reviewed journals or by attending conferences where new research is presented and ideas are exchanged. Informal methods of communication also exist, and not all members of a coherent community share all their work with one another for various professional reasons. Unlike earlier centuries, when scholars were members of learned societies or similar institutions, there is no single body today that represents all of science. In the United States, the National Academy of Sciences sometimes acts as a representative when policymakers or the government seek the opinions of the scientific community. However, the statements of the National Academy are not binding on scientists and do not necessarily reflect the views of every scientist. Nevertheless, the concept of scientific consensus is often invoked when addressing questions that can be examined through scientific methodology. While it is not always easy to determine the consensus opinion of the community, the standards and utility of the scientific method generally ensure agreement on a mainstream body of facts supported by scientific theory, while rejecting ideas that contradict this understanding. Scientific consensus is crucial for science education, evaluating new ideas, and research funding. Critics of scientific consensus often argue that there is a bias within the community against new ideas, as seen in discussions about protoscience, fringe science, and pseudoscience. In response, skeptical organizations have dedicated significant resources to debunking claims that challenge scientific consensus. Philosophers of science debate the epistemological limits of consensus, with figures like Thomas Kuhn highlighting the occurrence of scientific revolutions in history as evidence that consensus can sometimes be incorrect. Despite this, the explanatory power of science, demonstrated by its ability to make accurate predictions and drive technological innovation, has solidified its status as a highly respected form of knowledge in both academia and popular culture. The high regard for scientific results in Western society has led to political controversies surrounding scientific topics. The perceived conflict between religion and science is often cited as a struggle between tradition and progress or faith and reason. This contentious relationship dates back to the early days of natural science, such as Galileo’s trial by the Inquisition for advocating heliocentrism. In more recent times, the creation-evolution controversy has seen religious believers in supernatural creation challenge the naturalistic explanations of origins provided by evolutionary biology, geology, and astronomy. While this dichotomy may appear different from a Continental European perspective, it persists and influences the semiotic framework represented by the scientific community in Europe. Following World War II, many scientists believed that nuclear power would resolve the impending energy crisis by providing energy that was too cheap to meter. This optimism led to the construction of numerous nuclear power plants but also sparked a global political movement opposing nuclear power due to safety concerns and its association with nuclear weapons. Mass protests in the United States and Europe during the 1970s and 1980s, along with the Chernobyl and Three Mile Island disasters, resulted in a decline in nuclear power plant construction. In recent decades, issues such as global warming and stem cell research have brought the opinions of the scientific community to the forefront of political debates.
